title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6981 – Reuters estimate
body: The fixing mechanism matters most right now because its message has shifted over the past month. For nearly a year, the PBOC has set its daily guidance weaker than market expectations, which traders read as an effort to slow the yuan's appreciation, and in late August that gap reached its widest since February, shortly after the yuan touched a three-and-a-half-year high. Through September, however, the midpoint has strengthened at a faster pace, narrowing its gap with market expectations and suggesting the central bank has eased its resistance to yuan gains. The fixing is still set weaker than models imply, so this looks like a loosening of the brakes rather than their removal. The balance Beijing is weighing is unchanged: a firmer currency supports capital stability and import costs, but too rapid a rise risks eroding export competitiveness while the domestic economy remains soft. The gap between each day's fixing and consensus estimates remains one of the clearest guides to how far the PBOC is willing to let the yuan run. --- Earlier: Goldman Sachs says yuan undervalued by up to 25% and markets underestimate how far it can rise --- The daily fixing is Beijing's quietest but clearest tool for telling markets how fast it wants the yuan to move, and after months of saying slow down, it has lately been saying go, gradually.Summary: The PBOC sets the daily USD/CNY reference rate, or midpoint, at around 0115 GMT, one of the most closely watched signals in Asian FX markets.

title: Goldman Sachs says yuan undervalued by up to 25% and markets underestimate how far it can rise
body: A gradual, policy-tolerated yuan appreciation would ripple through Asian FX, with currencies tied closely to China's trade cycle likely to benefit from a firmer anchor in the region. A stronger yuan against the euro and dollar would ease some trade tensions but also squeeze margins for Chinese exporters, shifting the advantage toward companies focused on higher-value technology and domestic demand. For global investors, the expected currency gain adds a return kicker to Chinese assets, potentially drawing inflows into onshore bonds and equities. The main risk to the view is the dollar itself, which has been supported by geopolitical tension and sticky inflation, so a renewed Iran war-driven oil spike that keeps the Fed hawkish could slow the yuan's ascent. --- Goldman thinks the yuan is one of the most underpriced bets in currency markets, and that Beijing is quietly coming round to the idea of letting it climb.

The warning that AI could shift income from labour to capital, and erode governments' main tax base, adds a longer-term fiscal risk for heavily indebted sovereigns. The view that the ECB needs far more market disorder before acting suggests investors should not count on an official backstop, leaving the spread vulnerable to headline swings until the 2027 election cycle. A constructive stance on core European rates, combined with neutrality on France, points to relative value trades favouring Bunds and other core markets over French debt while uncertainty persists. --- Goldman reckons France's bond spread is now hostage to oil, the ECB and the 2027 ballot box, and none of those is likely to come to the rescue soon.

title: More on Standard Chartered adding RLUSD custody in Dubai, eyes LMAX collateral link for clients
body: The announcement is more a signal about market structure than a price catalyst. Bank custody does not create direct demand for RLUSD or for XRP, and traders should not read it that way. The bigger question is competition. If regulated banks start offering off-exchange margin, smaller stablecoins with bank backing could win institutional business that has so far gone to the largest tokens. Venues may also come under pressure to offer similar setups once a mirrored model proves itself, which could change how collateral moves across crypto trading. --- Earlier: Standard Chartered custody for Ripple's RLUSD: what custody and collateral mirroring mean for traders --- Standard Chartered is offering to hold Ripple's stablecoin and let clients trade against it without the tokens ever reaching an exchange, but the trading half of that promise still needs regulators to sign off. Summary: Standard Chartered now offers institutional custody of RLUSD on the XRP Ledger through its DIFC branch, regulated by the DFSA. A planned integration with LMAX Group would make RLUSD eligible collateral on agreed LMAX products through "collateral mirroring." Under mirroring, the tokens stay at the bank while LMAX credits their value toward client positions. The LMAX leg is not live and still needs final documentation, testing and regulatory approval, with no launch date given. RLUSD has a market value of about $2.45 billion, under 1% of a roughly $306 billion stablecoin market.

title: Saudi Arabia eyes 1.2 million bpd pipeline boost within weeks by converting gas line
body: A quick 1.2 million bpd addition to bypass capacity would ease some of the supply-risk premium built into crude, since it widens the route Saudi barrels can take around a disrupted Strait of Hormuz. The bearish oil price read is tempered by execution risk: the same corridor was knocked offline by a drone strike only last month, and Houthi attacks keep the Red Sea leg exposed. Port capacity at Yanbu is the bigger constraint for traders to watch, because extra pipeline volume only reaches the market if loadings can keep pace. Taken together, the plan signals that Riyadh expects disruption at Hormuz to persist, and that is supportive of prices over the longer run even if the near-term supply outlook improves at the margin. ---- Earlier: Big Monday recap... Oil gains on two fronts as Russia hits Ukraine and Saudi vows Houthi response --- Riyadh is reaching for the fastest lever it has to get more crude around Hormuz, though the real bottleneck may sit at the Red Sea port rather than in the pipe.

title: Standard Chartered custody for Ripple's RLUSD: what custody and collateral mirroring mean for traders
body: Standard Chartered will now hold Ripple's dollar-pegged stablecoin, RLUSD, for institutional clients through its branch in the Dubai International Financial Centre. The bank also plans to let those clients use RLUSD as trading collateral at LMAX Group without the tokens ever leaving the bank. That second part is not live yet. Together, though, the two pieces show how traditional finance is trying to fix one of crypto's oldest problems: what happens to your money when the venue holding it fails. To see why this matters, it helps to unpack three ideas: stablecoins, custody and collateral. What happened The bank announced on Monday that it now supports institutional custody of RLUSD issued on the XRP Ledger. The service runs through its DIFC branch, which is regulated by the Dubai Financial Services Authority. Separately, Standard Chartered has joined a planned integration with LMAX Group, a London-based marketplace for currencies and crypto, that would make RLUSD eligible collateral on agreed LMAX products. What is RLUSD? A stablecoin is a crypto token designed to hold a steady value, in this case $1. RLUSD is backed by US dollars, US government bonds and cash equivalents. Ripple launched it in December 2024 on both Ethereum and the XRP Ledger, a public blockchain closely associated with Ripple. The bank's new service covers only the XRP Ledger version. RLUSD has grown to a market value of roughly $2.45 billion.

A deeper negative print in the PPI suggests that cost pressures for producers continued to ease, which can provide some relief for input-heavy industries but may also signal weak pricing power and subdued demand. Market participants are likely to watch upcoming data closely to assess whether this decline in producer prices feeds through to broader inflation dynamics in Japan. Transportation costs were the biggest driver of inflation, contributing 1.13 percentage points to the overall rate. The government is set to raise fuel prices in October, after keeping them unchanged in September despite sharply higher global crude oil prices. At the same time, price declines across several food categories helped temper inflationary pressures in September. Over the first nine months of the year, inflation averaged 2.26%, with housing rents emerging as the largest single contributor, adding 0.72 percentage points. On a monthly basis, the consumer price index (CPI) increased by 0.16% in September—its first monthly rise in three months—following a 0.25% decline in August.
